### abstract.tex
\begin{abstract}
Test-time scaling through multi-sample generation promises quality improvements for LLM-based information extraction, but which confidence signals best serve quality estimation versus sample selection remains unclear.
We systematically compare five confidence signals from three families---structural (entity voting, Soft Jaccard), surface (exact match, Fleiss' $\kappa$), and model-internal (log-probability)---across NER and relation extraction on three datasets (SciERC, CoNLL-2003, WNUT-17) with two model families (Qwen3-8B, LLaMA-3.1-8B).
We find that the strongest signals achieve $\rho{=}0.38$ (entity voting) and AUROC${=}0.75$ (exact match) for quality estimation, with ranking and classification favoring different signals across task complexity; however, this strong quality estimation does not translate into selection gains---no signal reliably surpasses greedy decoding on either task ($p{>}0.39$, bootstrap) despite 13--18~pp of oracle headroom.

Signal rankings further depend on task difficulty---exact match dominates easy tasks, structural signals dominate hard tasks, and all signals converge when model capability is insufficient---establishing that signal choice should be guided by task difficulty and intended application.
These results reframe consistency signals as quality estimators rather than output selectors for structured IE.
\end{abstract}

1	\section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}
2	
3	Self-consistency---sampling multiple outputs and aggregating them---has become a powerful strategy for improving language model reasoning.
4	On discrete-answer tasks such as arithmetic and commonsense QA, majority voting over chain-of-thought samples yields large gains: +18 percentage points on GSM8K \cite{wang2023selfconsistency}.
5	More broadly, test-time compute scaling through repeated sampling and selection has emerged as a complementary axis to model scaling, offering substantial quality improvements at inference time \cite{snell2024scaling, brown2024monkeys}.
6	These results rest on a shared assumption: that among $N$ stochastic samples, a selection mechanism can identify better outputs.
7	For tasks with a single correct answer, this assumption holds naturally---the majority vote is the selector.
8	But information extraction (IE) poses a fundamentally different challenge.
9	The output is not a single token or number; it is a \textit{set} of entities or relations with internal dependencies, where two samples may extract overlapping but non-identical structures.
10	There is no obvious majority to vote on, partial agreement is the norm rather than the exception, and the space of valid outputs is combinatorially large.
11	Can self-consistency still provide useful signal in this structured setting?
12	
13	Prior work on confidence estimation for LLM-based IE has conflated two distinct objectives.
14	\textit{Quality estimation} asks which inputs the model handles reliably---a ranking over instances.
15	\textit{Sample selection} asks which of $N$ candidate outputs is best for a given input---a ranking over samples.
16	These require fundamentally different signal properties: the former benefits from instance-level aggregation across all $N$ samples, while the latter demands per-sample discrimination.
17	Existing evaluations rarely separate the two.
18	Self-consistency methods designed for discrete answers \cite{wang2023selfconsistency, chen2024usc} assume outputs can be grouped by equivalence and counted, an assumption that breaks when outputs are entity sets with partial overlap.
19	Weighted variants that incorporate model confidence \cite{taubenfeld2025cisc, kang2025selfcertainty} have shown promise for best-of-$N$ selection on reasoning tasks, but their applicability to structured prediction remains untested.
20	The most directly relevant study, \citet{nedellec2026consistency}, examines consistency--accuracy correlations for LLM-based entity and relation extraction but relies on surface-level matching, a limitation the authors themselves acknowledge: their approach ``overlooks semantically consistent outputs'' that differ only in surface form.
21	No existing work systematically compares confidence signals across the structural, surface, and model-internal families for generative IE, nor disentangles quality estimation from sample selection in this setting.
22	
23	Our central finding is that consistency-based signals are effective instance-level quality estimators but poor sample selectors for structured IE.
24	Consistency signals aggregate over $N$ samples to produce a single score per input, making them well-suited to predict input difficulty---instances where the model consistently extracts similar structures are indeed easier.
25	Entity voting confidence achieves the strongest rank correlation (Spearman $\rho{=}0.38$) on SciERC NER, while exact match leads binary discrimination (AUROC${=}0.75$), both strong enough to be practically useful for quality-aware routing.
26	Yet this correlation does not translate into substantial selection gains: no signal reliably surpasses greedy decoding on either NER or RE best-of-$N$ ($p{>}0.39$, bootstrap) despite 13--18 percentage points of oracle headroom.
27	We term this the \textbf{correlation-selection gap} (Figure~\ref{fig:overview}).
28	The gap arises because instance-level signals cannot discriminate among $N$ candidates that share similar consistency profiles---they predict \textit{which inputs} are hard, not \textit{which output} is best.
29	
30	\begin{figure*}[t]
31	\centering
32	\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{fig_overview}
33	\caption{The correlation-selection gap. Left: consistency signals (here Soft Jaccard) predict instance-level quality---high agreement correlates with high F1 ($\rho{\approx}0.39$, AUROC${\approx}0.70$). Right: the same instance-level signal assigns identical scores to all $N$ candidates from a given input, precluding sample selection. No signal reliably surpasses greedy on either task ($p{=}0.39$ for NER logprob).}
34	\label{fig:overview}
35	\end{figure*}
36	
37	We systematically evaluate five confidence signals from three families---structural (entity voting, Soft Jaccard), surface (exact match, Fleiss' $\kappa$), and model-internal (log-probability)---across NER and RE on SciERC \cite{luan2018scierc}, CoNLL-2003 \cite{tjongkimsang2003conll}, and WNUT-17 \cite{derczynski2017wnut}, using Qwen3-8B and LLaMA-3.1-8B.
38	
39	Our contributions are as follows:
40	\begin{enumerate}
41	    \item \textbf{First systematic comparison of confidence signals for generative IE.}
42	    We evaluate five signals from three families on quality estimation for NER and RE.
43	    Entity voting achieves the strongest $\rho{=}0.38$ while exact match leads AUROC${=}0.75$; signal rankings depend on both task complexity and evaluation metric, with structural signals leading rank correlation on complex schemas (SciERC) and surface signals leading on simpler tasks (CoNLL).
44	
45	    \item \textbf{Identification of the correlation-selection gap.}
46	    We demonstrate a fundamental disconnect between quality estimation and sample selection in structured IE.
47	    Despite strong instance-level correlations ($\rho$ up to 0.38), no signal reliably surpasses greedy on either task ($p{>}0.39$, bootstrap) despite 13--18~pp of oracle headroom.
48	    This gap reflects the instance-level nature of consistency signals, which predict input difficulty rather than discriminating among individual samples.
49	
50	    \item \textbf{Task-complexity boundary conditions.}
51	    Signal rankings depend on task difficulty: exact match leads on easy tasks (CoNLL), Soft Jaccard dominates on hard tasks (SciERC), and all signals converge when model capability is insufficient (WNUT-17, where 54\% of instances receive zero F1).
52	    This establishes practical guidance for signal selection based on expected task difficulty.
53	\end{enumerate}
54	
55	The remainder of this paper is organized as follows.
56	\S\ref{sec:method} formalizes the problem and defines the five confidence signals.
57	\S\ref{sec:experiments} presents quality estimation results, the correlation-selection gap analysis, and robustness evaluations.
58	\S\ref{sec:related} situates our work in the broader landscape of self-consistency, uncertainty estimation, and LLM-based IE.

On discrete-answer tasks such as arithmetic and commonsense QA, majority voting over chain-of-thought samples yields large gains: +18 percentage points on GSM8K \cite{wang2023selfconsistency}.

These results rest on a shared assumption: that among $N$ stochastic samples, a selection mechanism can identify better outputs.
For tasks with a single correct answer, this assumption holds naturally---the majority vote is the selector.
But information extraction (IE) poses a fundamentally different challenge.
The output is not a single token or number; it is a \textit{set} of entities or relations with internal dependencies, where two samples may extract overlapping but non-identical structures.
There is no obvious majority to vote on, partial agreement is the norm rather than the exception, and the space of valid outputs is combinatorially large.
Can self-consistency still provide useful signal in this structured setting?

Prior work on confidence estimation for LLM-based IE has conflated two distinct objectives.
\textit{Quality estimation} asks which inputs the model handles reliably---a ranking over instances.
\textit{Sample selection} asks which of $N$ candidate outputs is best for a given input---a ranking over samples.

Existing evaluations rarely separate the two.
Self-consistency methods designed for discrete answers \cite{wang2023selfconsistency, chen2024usc} assume outputs can be grouped by equivalence and counted, an assumption that breaks when outputs are entity sets with partial overlap.
Weighted variants that incorporate model confidence \cite{taubenfeld2025cisc, kang2025selfcertainty} have shown promise for best-of-$N$ selection on reasoning tasks, but their applicability to structured prediction remains untested.
The most directly relevant study, \citet{nedellec2026consistency}, examines consistency--accuracy correlations for LLM-based entity and relation extraction but relies on surface-level matching, a limitation the authors themselves acknowledge: their approach ``overlooks semantically consistent outputs'' that differ only in surface form.
No existing work systematically compares confidence signals across the structural, surface, and model-internal families for generative IE, nor disentangles quality estimation from sample selection in this setting.

Our central finding is that consistency-based signals are effective instance-level quality estimators but poor sample selectors for structured IE.
Consistency signals aggregate over $N$ samples to produce a single score per input, making them well-suited to predict input difficulty---instances where the model consistently extracts similar structures are indeed easier.
Entity voting confidence achieves the strongest rank correlation (Spearman $\rho{=}0.38$) on SciERC NER, while exact match leads binary discrimination (AUROC${=}0.75$), both strong enough to be practically useful for quality-aware routing.
Yet this correlation does not translate into substantial selection gains: no signal reliably surpasses greedy decoding on either NER or RE best-of-$N$ ($p{>}0.39$, bootstrap) despite 13--18 percentage points of oracle headroom.
We term this the \textbf{correlation-selection gap} (Figure~\ref{fig:overview}).
The gap arises because instance-level signals cannot discriminate among $N$ candidates that share similar consistency profiles---they predict \textit{which inputs} are hard, not \textit{which output} is best.

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{fig_overview}
\caption{The correlation-selection gap. Left: consistency signals (here Soft Jaccard) predict instance-level quality---high agreement correlates with high F1 ($\rho{\approx}0.39$, AUROC${\approx}0.70$). Right: the same instance-level signal assigns identical scores to all $N$ candidates from a given input, precluding sample selection. No signal reliably surpasses greedy on either task ($p{=}0.39$ for NER logprob).}
\label{fig:overview}
\end{figure*}

We systematically evaluate five confidence signals from three families---structural (entity voting, Soft Jaccard), surface (exact match, Fleiss' $\kappa$), and model-internal (log-probability)---across NER and RE on SciERC \cite{luan2018scierc}, CoNLL-2003 \cite{tjongkimsang2003conll}, and WNUT-17 \cite{derczynski2017wnut}, using Qwen3-8B and LLaMA-3.1-8B.

Our contributions are as follows:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{First systematic comparison of confidence signals for generative IE.}
    We evaluate five signals from three families on quality estimation for NER and RE.
    Entity voting achieves the strongest $\rho{=}0.38$ while exact match leads AUROC${=}0.75$; signal rankings depend on both task complexity and evaluation metric, with structural signals leading rank correlation on complex schemas (SciERC) and surface signals leading on simpler tasks (CoNLL).

    \item \textbf{Identification of the correlation-selection gap.}
    We demonstrate a fundamental disconnect between quality estimation and sample selection in structured IE.
    Despite strong instance-level correlations ($\rho$ up to 0.38), no signal reliably surpasses greedy on either task ($p{>}0.39$, bootstrap) despite 13--18~pp of oracle headroom.
    This gap reflects the instance-level nature of consistency signals, which predict input difficulty rather than discriminating among individual samples.

    \item \textbf{Task-complexity boundary conditions.}
    Signal rankings depend on task difficulty: exact match leads on easy tasks (CoNLL), Soft Jaccard dominates on hard tasks (SciERC), and all signals converge when model capability is insufficient (WNUT-17, where 54\% of instances receive zero F1).
    This establishes practical guidance for signal selection based on expected task difficulty.
\end{enumerate}

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows.
\S\ref{sec:method} formalizes the problem and defines the five confidence signals.
\S\ref{sec:experiments} presents quality estimation results, the correlation-selection gap analysis, and robustness evaluations.
\S\ref{sec:related} situates our work in the broader landscape of self-consistency, uncertainty estimation, and LLM-based IE.

1	\section{Method}\label{sec:method}
2	
3	We present a framework for evaluating confidence signals in test-time scaling for information extraction.
4	This section formalizes the problem (\S\ref{sec:formulation}), defines five confidence signals spanning three families (\S\ref{sec:signals}), and introduces the evaluation protocol (\S\ref{sec:evaluation}).
5	
6	\subsection{Problem Formulation}\label{sec:formulation}
7	
8	Given a language model $\mathcal{M}$ and an input instance $x$, we independently sample $N$ structured outputs $\{y_1, \ldots, y_N\}$ at temperature $T > 0$.
9	Each $y_i$ is a structured extraction result---an entity set for NER or a relation set for RE---produced via constrained decoding \cite{willard2023guided} to ensure valid output structure.
10	Our goal is to define a confidence signal $c$ that serves two purposes: (a) \textit{quality estimation}---predicting which instances the model handles reliably, and (b) \textit{sample selection}---identifying the best output among the $N$ candidates.
11	
12	A key distinction underlies this framework.
13	A \textbf{per-sample signal} scores each $y_i$ independently, $c_{\text{ps}}: (x, y_i) \to \mathbb{R}$, enabling direct ranking of the $N$ candidates.
14	An \textbf{instance-level signal} aggregates over all $N$ samples, $c_{\text{il}}: (x, \{y_i\}_{i=1}^N) \to \mathbb{R}$, producing a single score per input.
15	Instance-level signals can estimate overall prediction reliability but do not inherently rank individual samples.
16	This asymmetry---between predicting \textit{which inputs} are easy and selecting \textit{which output} is best---is central to the correlation-selection gap we investigate.
17	
18	Table~\ref{tab:notation} summarizes our notation.
19	
20	\begin{table}[h]
21	\centering
22	\small
23	\begin{tabular}{cl}
24	\toprule
25	Symbol & Meaning \\
26	\midrule
27	$\mathcal{M}$ & Language model \\
28	$x$ & Input instance \\
29	$y_i$ & $i$-th stochastic sample \\
30	$N$ & Number of samples \\
31	$T$ & Sampling temperature \\
32	$c(\cdot)$ & Confidence signal \\
33	SJ & Soft Jaccard similarity \\
34	FK & Fleiss' $\kappa$ \\
35	EM & Exact-match voting rate \\
36	$c_{\text{vote}}$ & Entity voting confidence \\
37	$c_{\text{lp}}$ & Log-probability (mean token log-likelihood) \\
38	\bottomrule
39	\end{tabular}
40	\caption{Notation used throughout the paper.}
41	\label{tab:notation}
42	\end{table}
43	
44	\subsection{Confidence Signals}\label{sec:signals}
45	
46	We compare five signals from three families: \textit{model-internal} (log-probability), \textit{surface} (exact match, Fleiss' $\kappa$), and \textit{structural} (Soft Jaccard, entity voting).
47	
48	\paragraph{Log-probability (model-internal, per-sample).}
49	The only per-sample signal in our comparison.
50	For a sample $y_i$ consisting of tokens $t_1, \ldots, t_{|y_i|}$, we define:
51	\begin{equation}\label{eq:logprob}
52	c_{\text{lp}}(y_i) = \frac{1}{|y_i|} \sum_{j=1}^{|y_i|} \log p_{\mathcal{M}}(t_j \mid t_{<j}, x)
53	\end{equation}
54	This is the length-normalized mean log-likelihood, reflecting the model's internal confidence in its generation.
55	Because it scores each sample independently, it can directly rank the $N$ candidates for sample selection.
56	
57	\paragraph{Exact match voting (surface, instance-level).}
58	Following self-consistency \cite{wang2023selfconsistency}, we define EM as the majority fraction---the proportion of samples producing the most common output:
59	\begin{equation}\label{eq:em}
60	c_{\text{em}}(x) = \frac{1}{N} \max_{y} \big|\{i : y_i = y\}\big|
61	\end{equation}
62	EM treats entire outputs as atomic units: two samples either match exactly or not, with no notion of partial overlap.
63	
64	\paragraph{Fleiss' $\kappa$ (surface, instance-level).}
65	We adapt the inter-rater agreement measure of \citet{fleiss1971agreement} to operate on extracted entity sets.
66	Unlike the classical token-level formulation, our items are the set of unique (text, type) entity tuples observed across all $N$ samples, and the $N$ samples serve as annotators who each assign a binary label---\textit{present} or \textit{absent}---to every entity, yielding a $|E_\cup| \times 2$ rating matrix:
67	\begin{equation}\label{eq:fk}
68	\kappa = \frac{\bar{P} - \bar{P}_e}{1 - \bar{P}_e}
69	\end{equation}
70	where $\bar{P}$ is the mean observed pairwise agreement rate across entities and $\bar{P}_e$ is the expected agreement under random assignment with the same marginal frequencies.
71	This entity-level binary formulation captures partial overlap between extraction sets: two samples sharing most entities but disagreeing on a few receive a moderately high $\kappa$.
72	Because it relies on exact string matching of entity mentions, FK does not tolerate near-synonym variations (e.g., ``machine learning'' vs.\ ``ML''), which the structural signals handle through soft span matching.
73	
74	\paragraph{Soft Jaccard (structural, instance-level).}
75	Our core structural signal extends Jaccard similarity \cite{jaccard1901distribution} to operate on extracted entity or relation \textit{sets} rather than raw strings.
76	For two samples $y_i$ and $y_j$, we first group extractions by entity type.
77	Within each group, we compute a bipartite matching using the Hungarian algorithm with span overlap as the similarity metric.
78	The pairwise Soft Jaccard score is:
79	\begin{equation}\label{eq:sj}
80	\text{SJ}(y_i, y_j) = \frac{\sum_{m \in M} \text{sim}(a_m, b_m)}{\sum_{g} \max(|g_i|, |g_j|)}
81	\end{equation}
82	where $M$ is the set of matched extraction pairs from the Hungarian algorithm, $\text{sim}(a_m, b_m)$ is the span-level Jaccard overlap between matched extractions, and $g_i$, $g_j$ index the extraction counts of samples $y_i$ and $y_j$ within entity type group $g$.
83	The numerator sums soft similarities rather than counting matches, allowing partial credit for near-overlapping spans.
84	The denominator uses $\max$ per type group rather than set union, which more heavily penalizes hallucinated extractions that inflate one sample's extraction count.
85	The instance-level signal averages over all sample pairs:
86	\begin{equation}\label{eq:sj_instance}
87	c_{\text{sj}}(x) = \frac{1}{\binom{N}{2}} \sum_{i<j} \text{SJ}(y_i, y_j)
88	\end{equation}
89	Two design choices distinguish SJ from surface signals.
90	First, type-aware grouping prevents spurious matches between extractions of different entity types.
91	Second, span-overlap matching tolerates near-synonym variations (e.g., ``machine learning'' vs.\ ``ML''), which would be penalized by exact string comparison.
92	
93	\paragraph{Entity voting confidence (structural, instance-level).}
94	While SJ compares entire extraction sets, entity voting operates at the granularity of individual extractions.
95	For each entity $e$ appearing in the union $E_\cup$ of all $N$ samples, we compute its frequency:
96	\begin{equation}\label{eq:freq}
97	\text{freq}(e) = \frac{|\{i : e \in y_i\}|}{N}
98	\end{equation}
99	The instance-level confidence is the mean frequency across all observed entities:
100	\begin{equation}\label{eq:voting}
101	c_{\text{vote}}(x) = \frac{1}{|E_\cup|} \sum_{e \in E_\cup} \text{freq}(e)
102	\end{equation}
103	This adapts majority voting \cite{wang2023selfconsistency} from discrete answer selection to set-valued extraction.
104	Entities that appear consistently across samples contribute high frequency; hallucinated or idiosyncratic extractions that appear in only one or two samples pull the score down.
105	This per-entity granularity enables the signal to distinguish instances where the model reliably extracts a core set of entities (high $c_{\text{vote}}$) from those where extractions vary widely across samples (low $c_{\text{vote}}$).
106	
107	\subsection{Evaluation Framework}\label{sec:evaluation}
108	
109	We assess confidence signals along two complementary dimensions.
110	
111	\paragraph{Quality estimation.}
112	Quality estimation asks: \textit{for which instances does the model produce reliable outputs?}
113	We measure rank correlation between the confidence signal and instance-level F1 via Spearman $\rho$.
114	For binary discrimination, we compute AUROC by classifying instances as above or below median F1.
115	These metrics evaluate whether a signal can identify reliable vs.\ unreliable predictions without access to gold labels.
116	
117	\paragraph{Sample selection.}
118	Sample selection asks: \textit{given $N$ candidates for a single instance, which one is best?}
119	We report best-of-$N$ F1: for each instance, the signal selects one sample, and we compute micro F1 over all instances.
120	We compare against an \textit{oracle} (which always selects the highest-F1 sample) and a \textit{greedy baseline} ($T{=}0$, $N{=}1$).
121	Per-sample signals like log-probability directly rank the $N$ candidates.
122	Instance-level signals (SJ, FK, EM, Voting) produce a single score per instance and thus require an auxiliary strategy for sample selection---we select the sample closest to the consensus output, i.e., the one with highest average pairwise similarity to all other samples.
123	
124	\paragraph{The two dimensions are complementary, not redundant.}
125	A signal with high rank correlation accurately predicts relative instance difficulty, making it useful for quality-aware routing or selective prediction.
126	However, high correlation does not guarantee effective sample selection: if per-sample variance is low---the model produces $N$ similar outputs for a given input---even a perfect quality estimator cannot distinguish among near-identical candidates.
127	We investigate this decoupling empirically in \S\ref{sec:selection_gap}.
128

1	\section{Experiments}
2	\label{sec:experiments}
3	
4	\subsection{Experimental Setup}
5	\label{sec:setup}
6	
7	\paragraph{Datasets.}
8	We evaluate on three English IE benchmarks spanning a difficulty gradient.
9	\textbf{SciERC} \cite{luan2018scierc} contains 551 test instances from scientific abstracts annotated for joint NER (6 entity types) and RE (7 relation types), representing a complex schema with overlapping structures.
10	\textbf{CoNLL-2003} \cite{tjongkimsang2003conll} provides 3{,}453 test sentences from newswire with 4 entity types, serving as a high-accuracy benchmark where models achieve ${>}$91\% micro F1.
11	\textbf{WNUT-17} \cite{derczynski2017wnut} consists of 1{,}287 test instances from social media with emerging entities, used to probe method boundaries where model capability is insufficient.
12	This gradient---from near-solved (CoNLL) through challenging (SciERC) to infeasible (WNUT-17)---enables systematic characterization of how signal effectiveness varies with task difficulty (\S\ref{sec:complexity_robustness}).
13	
14	\paragraph{Models.}
15	Our primary model is \textbf{Qwen3-8B}, fine-tuned with LoRA ($r{=}32$) separately per dataset.
16	For cross-model validation, we evaluate \textbf{LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct} to assess whether structural confidence signals transfer across architectures and training regimes.
17	
18	\paragraph{Sampling and Evaluation.}
19	For each test instance, we draw $N$ independent samples at temperature $T{=}1.0$, with $T{=}0.7$ for robustness analysis.
20	We use $N{=}8$ for both SciERC and CoNLL in the primary evaluation, and $N{=}16$ for SciERC scaling experiments.\footnote{$N{=}16$ experiments for CoNLL (Qwen) and SciERC (LLaMA) have also been completed with consistent results; see Table~\ref{tab:robustness}.}
21	Quality estimation is measured along two axes: \textit{rank correlation} with instance-level F1 via Spearman $\rho$, and \textit{binary discrimination} via AUROC (instances above vs.\ below median F1).
22	Downstream utility is assessed through \textbf{best-of-$N$ selection F1}: the F1 obtained when each signal selects one sample per instance.
23	Instance-level F1 uses exact span matching for NER and head-tail-label matching for RE, where a relation is correct only when both argument entities and the relation label match the gold annotation.
24	The greedy decoding baseline ($T{=}0$, $N{=}1$) establishes performance without test-time scaling.
25	
26	\paragraph{Confidence Signals.}
27	We compare five signals from three families (detailed in \S\ref{sec:signals}).
28	\textit{Structural} signals operate on extracted entity/relation sets: \textbf{Voting Confidence} aggregates per-extraction frequency across samples, and \textbf{Soft Jaccard (SJ)} measures pairwise set similarity \cite{jaccard1901distribution}.
29	\textit{Surface} signals operate on string representations: \textbf{Fleiss' $\kappa$ (FK)} quantifies inter-sample agreement treating samples as independent annotators \cite{fleiss1971agreement}, and \textbf{Exact Match (EM)} computes the fraction of identical sample pairs.
30	The \textit{model-internal} signal is \textbf{log-probability (logprob)}, the mean token-level log-likelihood.
31	
32	\paragraph{Implementation.}
33	Inference uses vLLM with XGrammar constrained decoding \cite{willard2023guided} to enforce valid JSON output structure.
34	A span realignment post-processing step corrects character-level offset mismatches between generated and gold annotation spans.
35	All confidence signals are computed from the $N$ samples without access to gold labels.
36	
37	%% ============================================================
38	\subsection{Quality Estimation Results}
39	\label{sec:qe_results}
40

SciERC evaluates joint NER (6 types) and RE (7 types); CoNLL evaluates NER (4 types). Primary results use $N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$; $N{=}16$ block reports LLaMA CoNLL 3-seed mean${\pm}$std.}

69	\begin{figure*}[t]

72	\caption{Quality estimation heatmap (Spearman $\rho$) across five signals and four configurations. Left: full evaluation set; right: conditional set (non-zero F1 instances). On the full set, structural signals dominate on SciERC while all signals converge on CoNLL. On the conditional set, EM emerges as the strongest signal on both NER ($\rho{=}0.408$) and RE ($\rho{=}0.485$), while logprob RE collapses to near-zero ($\rho{=}0.002$).}
73	\label{fig:signal_heatmap}

75	
76	Table~\ref{tab:quality_estimation} presents rank correlation ($\rho$) and AUROC for five confidence signals across tasks and models.
77	
78	\paragraph{Structural signals dominate on complex schemas.}
79	On SciERC NER, structural signals form a leading cluster: Voting Confidence achieves $\rho{=}0.379$ and SJ reaches $\rho{=}0.360$, both outperforming surface signals ($\rho{\leq}0.295$) and log-probability ($\rho{=}0.205$).
80	The Voting--SJ gap ($\Delta\rho{=}0.019$) is within bootstrap uncertainty, suggesting that both structural signals capture similar quality-relevant information at different granularities: Voting rewards per-entity consistency while SJ compares entire extraction sets.
81	The structural advantage persists on RE, where Voting ($\rho{=}0.422$) again leads.
82	However, all signals weaken on RE: 44\% of instances receive zero F1, creating a floor effect that compresses the discriminable range.
83	Notably, FK ($\rho{=}0.253$) exceeds SJ ($\rho{=}0.211$) on RE---a reversal from NER that shows no single structural signal dominates across both tasks.
84	
85	\paragraph{$\rho$--AUROC dissociation.}
86	AUROC rankings on SciERC diverge from $\rho$ rankings.
87	On NER, EM leads AUROC (0.749) despite ranking third in $\rho$ (0.295), while Voting---the $\rho$ leader (0.379)---drops to third in AUROC (0.684).
88	On RE, the dissociation is more extreme: EM achieves the highest AUROC (0.706) while ranking last in $\rho$ (0.100).
89	Binary agreement provides clean separation between reliable and unreliable instances (high AUROC), while structural signals capture finer-grained quality variation (high $\rho$).
90	This dissociation recurs on CoNLL with log-probability (see below), suggesting it reflects fundamental differences between ranking and classification rather than dataset-specific effects.
91	
92	\paragraph{Signal rankings shift with task difficulty.}
93	On CoNLL NER, where greedy decoding achieves ${>}$91\% micro F1, the signal landscape changes substantially.
94	Exact Match leads with $\rho{=}0.451$ and AUROC${=}0.816$, surpassing SJ ($\rho{=}0.436$) and Voting ($\rho{=}0.424$).
95	When most samples are near-correct, binary agreement captures the remaining variance more efficiently than set-level similarity.
96	This reversal---EM${>}$SJ on easy tasks vs.\ SJ${>}$EM on hard tasks---demonstrates that optimal signal choice depends on intrinsic task difficulty.
97	
98	\paragraph{Cross-model stability.}
99	Comparing Qwen and LLaMA on CoNLL, SJ shows remarkable stability: $\rho{=}0.436$ (Qwen) vs.\ $\rho{=}0.431$ (LLaMA), a gap of only 0.005.
100	This model-agnostic property is expected for structural signals that operate on outputs rather than internal model states, and provides the strongest evidence that SJ generalizes across architectures.
101	The SJ--FK gap also narrows with schema simplification: $\Delta\rho{=}0.093$ on SciERC NER (6 entity types) vs.\ $\Delta\rho{=}0.003$ on CoNLL with LLaMA (4 types), suggesting that set-level structure contributes less when the type inventory is small.
102	
103	\paragraph{The logprob paradox.}
104	Log-probability reveals an additional instance of the $\rho$--AUROC dissociation.
105	On CoNLL with LLaMA, it achieves the highest AUROC (0.761) yet the lowest $\rho$ (0.307) among all signals.
106	This pattern---strong binary discrimination paired with weak ranking---parallels EM's behavior on SciERC and indicates that logprob assigns well-separated scores to easy vs.\ hard instances but provides little resolution within each group, making it better suited for binary filtering than continuous quality estimation.
107	We return to this distinction in \S\ref{sec:complexity_robustness} and visualize it in Figure~\ref{fig:signal_heatmap}.
108	
109	\paragraph{Oracle headroom and practical ceilings.}
110	On CoNLL, oracle best-of-$N$ selection yields only +4.2~pp (Qwen) and +1.8~pp (LLaMA) over greedy.
111	When the model already operates near its performance ceiling, confidence signals serve as \textit{reliability assurance}---confirming that outputs are trustworthy---rather than enabling selective prediction gains.
112	We therefore focus selection analysis (\S\ref{sec:selection_gap}) on SciERC, where oracle headroom exceeds 13~pp.
113	
114	%% ============================================================
115	\subsection{The Correlation-Selection Gap}
116	\label{sec:selection_gap}
117	
118	\begin{figure*}[t]

121	\caption{The correlation-selection gap on SciERC ($N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$). Left: NER; right: RE. Bars show best-of-$N$ selection F1; the line marks quality estimation $\rho$. Despite $\rho$ up to 0.38, no signal reliably surpasses greedy on either task ($p{=}0.39$ for NER logprob, the best signal). Dashed line indicates oracle upper bound.}
122	\label{fig:selection_gap}
123	\end{figure*}
124	
125	\begin{table}[t]
126	\centering
127	\small
128	\caption{Best-of-$N$ selection F1 on SciERC ($N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$). Best non-oracle result per column in \textbf{bold}. EM produces binary agreement without sample ranking.}
129	\label{tab:selection}
130	\begin{tabular}{lcc}
131	\toprule
132	Method & NER F1 & RE F1 \\
133	\midrule
134	Oracle & 0.776 & 0.585 \\
135	\midrule
136	Log-prob           & \textbf{0.650} & 0.395 \\
137	Soft Jaccard       & 0.645 & 0.386 \\
138	Voting             & 0.634 & 0.359 \\
139	Exact Match        & ---   & ---   \\
140	\midrule
141	Greedy ($T{=}0$)   & 0.644 & \textbf{0.404} \\
142	Random             & 0.608 & 0.354 \\
143	\bottomrule
144	\end{tabular}
145	\end{table}
146	
147	Despite strong quality estimation, confidence signals yield limited gains when used for best-of-$N$ selection.
148	Table~\ref{tab:selection} compares selection F1 on SciERC ($N{=}8$).
149	
150	\paragraph{NER: no signal reliably surpasses greedy.}
151	The oracle upper bound (0.776) reveals 13.2~pp of headroom above greedy (0.644), confirming that substantially better candidates exist among the $N$ samples.
152	Log-probability achieves the highest point estimate (0.650, +0.6~pp over greedy), but this difference is not statistically significant ($p{=}0.39$, 3-seed bootstrap 95\% CI: [$-$3.0, +4.2]~pp, Cohen's $d{=}0.038$; sign test: 61W/70L, win\%${=}$46.6\%).
153	SJ (0.645) and all other signals are similarly non-significant ($p{>}0.5$).
154	Voting ($\rho{=}0.379$, the best quality estimator) selects to only 0.634, \textit{below} greedy.
155	The Random baseline (0.608) confirms that not all samples are equal---uniform selection loses 3.6~pp vs.\ greedy---but the discriminative structure captured by confidence signals adds no reliable value beyond greedy's deterministic choice.
156	
157	\paragraph{RE: no signal surpasses greedy.}
158	On RE, the correlation-selection gap is complete: no signal exceeds greedy (0.404).
159	Log-probability selects to 0.395 ($-$0.9~pp) and SJ to 0.386 ($-$1.9~pp), despite an oracle gap of 18.1~pp (0.585 vs.\ 0.404) indicating substantial per-instance variance.
160	Unlike NER, where logprob's per-token evaluation provides marginal selection value, compound entity-then-relation decisions create extraction errors that even per-sample signals cannot diagnose: a sample may have high token-level confidence yet extract the wrong relation arguments.
161	
162	\paragraph{Quality estimation $\neq$ output selection.}
163	We attribute this gap (Figure~\ref{fig:selection_gap}) to a fundamental distinction: instance-level confidence signals predict \textit{which inputs} the model handles reliably, not \textit{which output} among $N$ candidates is best for a given input.
164	When per-sample variance is low relative to instance-level difficulty---as in NER, where the model often produces $N$ similar extractions---even perfect quality estimation cannot discriminate among near-identical candidates.
165	
166	\paragraph{Implications for test-time scaling.}
167	This correlation-selection gap has direct consequences for test-time scaling in IE \cite{brown2024monkeys, snell2024scaling}.
168	Scaling inference compute through repeated sampling assumes a selector can identify the best sample.
169	Our results show that for structured prediction, existing confidence signals serve as quality \textit{estimators}---useful for flagging unreliable predictions---but not as effective \textit{selectors}.
170	Closing this gap likely requires signals that capture per-sample rather than per-instance variation, such as trained verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers} or pairwise comparison models.
171	
172	%% ============================================================
173	\subsection{Task Complexity and Signal Robustness}
174	\label{sec:complexity_robustness}
175	
176	\paragraph{Task difficulty as a boundary condition.}
177	Signal effectiveness varies systematically with task difficulty.
178	On CoNLL (greedy micro F1${>}$0.91), EM leads all signals ($\rho{=}0.451$); on SciERC NER (micro F1$\,{\approx}\,$0.66), SJ overtakes EM ($\rho{=}0.360$ vs.\ 0.295); on SciERC RE, where 44\% of instances score zero F1, all signals converge to $\rho{\approx}0.25$.
179	The NER--RE difference is statistically confirmed: Fisher's $z$-test on $\rho_\text{SJ}$ yields $z{=}2.31$, $p{=}0.021$.
180	
181	\paragraph{Per-relation diagnostic.}
182	RE signal degradation is relation-specific.
183	\textsc{Feature-Of} has near-zero correlation ($\rho{=}0.004$), while \textsc{Hyponym-Of} achieves $\rho{=}0.646$.
184	The primary bottleneck is entity span errors, which account for 55.5\% of RE false negatives---a prerequisite failure that consistency signals cannot detect, as they measure agreement among equally incorrect extractions.
185	We note that RE analysis relies on a single dataset (SciERC); generalization to other RE benchmarks remains to be validated.
186	
187	\paragraph{Capability stratification.}
188	For NER, SJ effectiveness scales with structural complexity: on SciERC instances with 6+ entities, $\rho{=}0.547$, compared to $\rho{=}0.415$ for 1--2 entities.
189	The SJ advantage over logprob remains stable across sentence-length quartiles ($\Delta\rho{\approx}0.08$--$0.20$).
190	For RE, SJ $\rho$ increases monotonically with sentence length (Q1: 0.110 $\to$ Q4: 0.473; Fisher $z$-test $p{=}0.004$), indicating that longer, more relation-dense sentences provide richer structure for consistency-based estimation.
191	Both proxies are weakly correlated with F1 ($|r|{<}0.15$), confirming they capture input complexity rather than directly predicting output quality; however, entity count and sentence length are themselves moderately correlated ($\rho{=}0.650$), so they reflect overlapping rather than independent complexity dimensions.
192	For RE, entity count and relation count are strongly correlated ($\rho{=}0.769$) and thus reflect a single structural complexity dimension rather than independent axes.
193	On the high-complexity RE subset ($n{=}81$, high relation count), signals improve substantially: Voting reaches $\rho{=}0.630$, logprob $\rho{=}0.554$, and SJ $\rho{=}0.502$---all far above the full-set levels.
194	Richer relational structure provides more signal for consistency-based estimation, complementing the task-level boundary established by WNUT-17: structural signals are most effective within a ``sweet spot'' of sufficient model capability and sufficient output complexity.
195	
196	\paragraph{Method boundary: WNUT-17.}
197	WNUT-17 establishes where the approach breaks down.
198	SJ achieves $\rho{=}0.062$ ($p{=}0.106$, not statistically significant), with 54\% of instances at zero F1.
199	Log-probability shows a strong \textit{negative} correlation: the model is confidently wrong on novel entities, a calibration failure that no post-hoc consistency signal can remedy.
200	This is a boundary of the method, not a limitation of the datasets.

251	FK $N$-scaling is inconsistent: degradation on SciERC ($-0.007$ to $-0.019$) but improvement on CoNLL with LLaMA ($+0.027$), suggesting sensitivity to both model and task characteristics.

260	On conditional RE (non-zero F1 instances), SJ recovers to $\rho{=}0.405$ while FK drops to $\rho{=}0.259$, confirming that structural advantage is robust across both models and evaluation conditions.
261	At $N{=}16$, the structural-over-logprob advantage holds across all four tested settings: Qwen SciERC (Voting $\rho{=}0.411$ vs.\ logprob 0.259, $\Delta{=}{+}0.152$), Qwen CoNLL (EM $\rho{=}0.463$ vs.\ logprob 0.328, $\Delta{=}{+}0.135$), LLaMA SciERC (Voting $\rho{=}0.452$ vs.\ logprob 0.277, $\Delta{=}{+}0.175$), and LLaMA CoNLL 3-seed (SJ $\rho{=}0.463{\pm}0.007$ vs.\ logprob $0.310{\pm}0.005$, $\Delta{=}{+}0.153$).

263	\paragraph{Evaluation circularity.}
264	Leave-one-out SJ (LOO-SJ), which excludes the target sample when computing confidence, yields $\Delta\rho{=}{-}0.014$ relative to standard SJ, with a maximum per-instance $\Delta\rho$ of $3.1{\times}10^{-4}$.
265	Evaluation circularity is negligible.

267	\paragraph{Conditional filtering reveals signal divergence.}
268	Filtering to non-zero F1 instances reshuffles signal rankings (Figure~\ref{fig:signal_heatmap}, right).
269	EM emerges as the strongest conditional signal on both NER ($\rho{=}0.408$) and RE ($\rho{=}0.485$), despite ranking third on the full NER set ($\rho{=}0.295$) and last on full RE ($\rho{=}0.100$).
270	This reversal extends EM's CoNLL dominance: once catastrophic failures are removed, the remaining instances produce mostly well-formed outputs where binary agreement is highly informative.
271	Conversely, Voting and FK---which derive much of their full-set correlation from the zero-vs-non-zero distinction---drop substantially on conditional (Voting NER: $0.379{\to}0.346$; FK NER: $0.267{\to}0.176$).
272	Log-probability on conditional RE collapses to $\rho{=}0.002$, confirming that its full-set correlation ($\rho{=}0.247$) was driven entirely by coarse separation between zero and non-zero F1 instances.
273	At $N{=}16$, the divergence persists: SJ maintains $\rho{=}0.308$ on conditional RE while logprob drops to $\rho{=}{-}0.026$.
274	This EM advantage on the conditional set is not SciERC-specific: EM ranks first across all four tested configurations---SciERC NER ($\rho{=}0.408$), CoNLL Qwen $N{=}16$ ($\rho{=}0.466$), CoNLL LLaMA 3-seed ($\rho{=}0.462$), and SciERC RE ($\rho{=}0.485$)---despite full-set rankings ranging from \#1 (CoNLL Qwen) to \#5 (SciERC RE).
275	On the full set, EM is diluted by trivial agreement: instances where all $N$ samples produce identical (possibly incorrect) outputs receive EM${=}1$ regardless of quality, compressing the signal's dynamic range.
276	On the conditional set---where the model demonstrably produces varied outputs---exact agreement becomes the strongest quality signal: ``the model gives the same answer despite being able to produce different ones'' is a more precise indicator than set-level similarity.
277	The margin over SJ is largest on RE ($\Delta\rho{=}{+}0.167$), where compound extraction decisions amplify output variability, and smallest on CoNLL LLaMA ($\Delta\rho{=}{+}0.002$), where all signals converge near $\rho{\approx}0.46$.
278	This creates a natural complementarity: Voting and SJ are preferred on the full set (handling both trivial and non-trivial instances), while EM provides the most precise quality ranking within the non-trivial subset.

286	
287	\paragraph{Binary filtering vs.\ continuous ranking.}
288	The $\rho$--AUROC dissociation---EM leading AUROC on SciERC while Voting leads $\rho$; logprob leading AUROC on CoNLL while ranking last in $\rho$---reflects a fundamental distinction in how signals encode quality information.
289	Signals suited for binary filtering (EM, logprob) provide coarse separation between reliable and unreliable instances, while structural signals like SJ and Voting provide finer-grained ranking suited for prioritization and quality-aware aggregation.
290	Figure~\ref{fig:reliability} visualizes this complementarity across the difficulty spectrum.
291	Practitioners should select signal type based on the downstream application: binary filtering favors EM or logprob depending on task complexity; ranking-dependent decisions favor structural consistency.

\section{Experiments}
\label{sec:experiments}

\subsection{Experimental Setup}
\label{sec:setup}

\paragraph{Datasets.}
We evaluate on three English IE benchmarks spanning a difficulty gradient.
\textbf{SciERC} \cite{luan2018scierc} contains 551 test instances from scientific abstracts annotated for joint NER (6 entity types) and RE (7 relation types), representing a complex schema with overlapping structures.
\textbf{CoNLL-2003} \cite{tjongkimsang2003conll} provides 3{,}453 test sentences from newswire with 4 entity types, serving as a high-accuracy benchmark where models achieve ${>}$91\% micro F1.
\textbf{WNUT-17} \cite{derczynski2017wnut} consists of 1{,}287 test instances from social media with emerging entities, used to probe method boundaries where model capability is insufficient.
This gradient---from near-solved (CoNLL) through challenging (SciERC) to infeasible (WNUT-17)---enables systematic characterization of how signal effectiveness varies with task difficulty (\S\ref{sec:complexity_robustness}).

\paragraph{Models.}
Our primary model is \textbf{Qwen3-8B}, fine-tuned with LoRA ($r{=}32$) separately per dataset.
For cross-model validation, we evaluate \textbf{LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct} to assess whether structural confidence signals transfer across architectures and training regimes.

\paragraph{Sampling and Evaluation.}
For each test instance, we draw $N$ independent samples at temperature $T{=}1.0$, with $T{=}0.7$ for robustness analysis.
We use $N{=}8$ for both SciERC and CoNLL in the primary evaluation, and $N{=}16$ for SciERC scaling experiments.\footnote{$N{=}16$ experiments for CoNLL (Qwen) and SciERC (LLaMA) have also been completed with consistent results; see Table~\ref{tab:robustness}.}
Quality estimation is measured along two axes: \textit{rank correlation} with instance-level F1 via Spearman $\rho$, and \textit{binary discrimination} via AUROC (instances above vs.\ below median F1).
Downstream utility is assessed through \textbf{best-of-$N$ selection F1}: the F1 obtained when each signal selects one sample per instance.
Instance-level F1 uses exact span matching for NER and head-tail-label matching for RE, where a relation is correct only when both argument entities and the relation label match the gold annotation.
The greedy decoding baseline ($T{=}0$, $N{=}1$) establishes performance without test-time scaling.

\paragraph{Confidence Signals.}
We compare five signals from three families (detailed in \S\ref{sec:signals}).
\textit{Structural} signals operate on extracted entity/relation sets: \textbf{Voting Confidence} aggregates per-extraction frequency across samples, and \textbf{Soft Jaccard (SJ)} measures pairwise set similarity \cite{jaccard1901distribution}.
\textit{Surface} signals operate on string representations: \textbf{Fleiss' $\kappa$ (FK)} quantifies inter-sample agreement treating samples as independent annotators \cite{fleiss1971agreement}, and \textbf{Exact Match (EM)} computes the fraction of identical sample pairs.
The \textit{model-internal} signal is \textbf{log-probability (logprob)}, the mean token-level log-likelihood.

\paragraph{Implementation.}
Inference uses vLLM with XGrammar constrained decoding \cite{willard2023guided} to enforce valid JSON output structure.
A span realignment post-processing step corrects character-level offset mismatches between generated and gold annotation spans.
All confidence signals are computed from the $N$ samples without access to gold labels.

%% ============================================================
\subsection{Quality Estimation Results}
\label{sec:qe_results}

On the conditional set, EM emerges as the strongest signal on both NER ($\rho{=}0.408$) and RE ($\rho{=}0.485$), while logprob RE collapses to near-zero ($\rho{=}0.002$).}

Table~\ref{tab:quality_estimation} presents rank correlation ($\rho$) and AUROC for five confidence signals across tasks and models.

\paragraph{Structural signals dominate on complex schemas.}
On SciERC NER, structural signals form a leading cluster: Voting Confidence achieves $\rho{=}0.379$ and SJ reaches $\rho{=}0.360$, both outperforming surface signals ($\rho{\leq}0.295$) and log-probability ($\rho{=}0.205$).
The Voting--SJ gap ($\Delta\rho{=}0.019$) is within bootstrap uncertainty, suggesting that both structural signals capture similar quality-relevant information at different granularities: Voting rewards per-entity consistency while SJ compares entire extraction sets.
The structural advantage persists on RE, where Voting ($\rho{=}0.422$) again leads.
However, all signals weaken on RE: 44\% of instances receive zero F1, creating a floor effect that compresses the discriminable range.
Notably, FK ($\rho{=}0.253$) exceeds SJ ($\rho{=}0.211$) on RE---a reversal from NER that shows no single structural signal dominates across both tasks.

\paragraph{$\rho$--AUROC dissociation.}
AUROC rankings on SciERC diverge from $\rho$ rankings.
On NER, EM leads AUROC (0.749) despite ranking third in $\rho$ (0.295), while Voting---the $\rho$ leader (0.379)---drops to third in AUROC (0.684).
On RE, the dissociation is more extreme: EM achieves the highest AUROC (0.706) while ranking last in $\rho$ (0.100).
Binary agreement provides clean separation between reliable and unreliable instances (high AUROC), while structural signals capture finer-grained quality variation (high $\rho$).
This dissociation recurs on CoNLL with log-probability (see below), suggesting it reflects fundamental differences between ranking and classification rather than dataset-specific effects.

\paragraph{Signal rankings shift with task difficulty.}
On CoNLL NER, where greedy decoding achieves ${>}$91\% micro F1, the signal landscape changes substantially.
Exact Match leads with $\rho{=}0.451$ and AUROC${=}0.816$, surpassing SJ ($\rho{=}0.436$) and Voting ($\rho{=}0.424$).
When most samples are near-correct, binary agreement captures the remaining variance more efficiently than set-level similarity.
This reversal---EM${>}$SJ on easy tasks vs.\ SJ${>}$EM on hard tasks---demonstrates that optimal signal choice depends on intrinsic task difficulty.

\paragraph{Cross-model stability.}
Comparing Qwen and LLaMA on CoNLL, SJ shows remarkable stability: $\rho{=}0.436$ (Qwen) vs.\ $\rho{=}0.431$ (LLaMA), a gap of only 0.005.
This model-agnostic property is expected for structural signals that operate on outputs rather than internal model states, and provides the strongest evidence that SJ generalizes across architectures.
The SJ--FK gap also narrows with schema simplification: $\Delta\rho{=}0.093$ on SciERC NER (6 entity types) vs.\ $\Delta\rho{=}0.003$ on CoNLL with LLaMA (4 types), suggesting that set-level structure contributes less when the type inventory is small.

\paragraph{The logprob paradox.}
Log-probability reveals an additional instance of the $\rho$--AUROC dissociation.
On CoNLL with LLaMA, it achieves the highest AUROC (0.761) yet the lowest $\rho$ (0.307) among all signals.
This pattern---strong binary discrimination paired with weak ranking---parallels EM's behavior on SciERC and indicates that logprob assigns well-separated scores to easy vs.\ hard instances but provides little resolution within each group, making it better suited for binary filtering than continuous quality estimation.
We return to this distinction in \S\ref{sec:complexity_robustness} and visualize it in Figure~\ref{fig:signal_heatmap}.

\paragraph{Oracle headroom and practical ceilings.}
On CoNLL, oracle best-of-$N$ selection yields only +4.2~pp (Qwen) and +1.8~pp (LLaMA) over greedy.
When the model already operates near its performance ceiling, confidence signals serve as \textit{reliability assurance}---confirming that outputs are trustworthy---rather than enabling selective prediction gains.
We therefore focus selection analysis (\S\ref{sec:selection_gap}) on SciERC, where oracle headroom exceeds 13~pp.

%% ============================================================
\subsection{The Correlation-Selection Gap}
\label{sec:selection_gap}

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering

\label{fig:selection_gap}
\end{figure*}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering

\midrule

\midrule

\end{table}

Despite strong quality estimation, confidence signals yield limited gains when used for best-of-$N$ selection.
Table~\ref{tab:selection} compares selection F1 on SciERC ($N{=}8$).

\paragraph{NER: no signal reliably surpasses greedy.}
The oracle upper bound (0.776) reveals 13.2~pp of headroom above greedy (0.644), confirming that substantially better candidates exist among the $N$ samples.
Log-probability achieves the highest point estimate (0.650, +0.6~pp over greedy), but this difference is not statistically significant ($p{=}0.39$, 3-seed bootstrap 95\% CI: [$-$3.0, +4.2]~pp, Cohen's $d{=}0.038$; sign test: 61W/70L, win\%${=}$46.6\%).
SJ (0.645) and all other signals are similarly non-significant ($p{>}0.5$).
Voting ($\rho{=}0.379$, the best quality estimator) selects to only 0.634, \textit{below} greedy.
The Random baseline (0.608) confirms that not all samples are equal---uniform selection loses 3.6~pp vs.\ greedy---but the discriminative structure captured by confidence signals adds no reliable value beyond greedy's deterministic choice.

\paragraph{RE: no signal surpasses greedy.}
On RE, the correlation-selection gap is complete: no signal exceeds greedy (0.404).
Log-probability selects to 0.395 ($-$0.9~pp) and SJ to 0.386 ($-$1.9~pp), despite an oracle gap of 18.1~pp (0.585 vs.\ 0.404) indicating substantial per-instance variance.
Unlike NER, where logprob's per-token evaluation provides marginal selection value, compound entity-then-relation decisions create extraction errors that even per-sample signals cannot diagnose: a sample may have high token-level confidence yet extract the wrong relation arguments.

\paragraph{Quality estimation $\neq$ output selection.}
We attribute this gap (Figure~\ref{fig:selection_gap}) to a fundamental distinction: instance-level confidence signals predict \textit{which inputs} the model handles reliably, not \textit{which output} among $N$ candidates is best for a given input.
When per-sample variance is low relative to instance-level difficulty---as in NER, where the model often produces $N$ similar extractions---even perfect quality estimation cannot discriminate among near-identical candidates.

\paragraph{Implications for test-time scaling.}
This correlation-selection gap has direct consequences for test-time scaling in IE \cite{brown2024monkeys, snell2024scaling}.
Scaling inference compute through repeated sampling assumes a selector can identify the best sample.
Our results show that for structured prediction, existing confidence signals serve as quality \textit{estimators}---useful for flagging unreliable predictions---but not as effective \textit{selectors}.
Closing this gap likely requires signals that capture per-sample rather than per-instance variation, such as trained verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers} or pairwise comparison models.

%% ============================================================
\subsection{Task Complexity and Signal Robustness}
\label{sec:complexity_robustness}

\paragraph{Task difficulty as a boundary condition.}
Signal effectiveness varies systematically with task difficulty.
On CoNLL (greedy micro F1${>}$0.91), EM leads all signals ($\rho{=}0.451$); on SciERC NER (micro F1$\,{\approx}\,$0.66), SJ overtakes EM ($\rho{=}0.360$ vs.\ 0.295); on SciERC RE, where 44\% of instances score zero F1, all signals converge to $\rho{\approx}0.25$.
The NER--RE difference is statistically confirmed: Fisher's $z$-test on $\rho_\text{SJ}$ yields $z{=}2.31$, $p{=}0.021$.

\paragraph{Per-relation diagnostic.}
RE signal degradation is relation-specific.
\textsc{Feature-Of} has near-zero correlation ($\rho{=}0.004$), while \textsc{Hyponym-Of} achieves $\rho{=}0.646$.
The primary bottleneck is entity span errors, which account for 55.5\% of RE false negatives---a prerequisite failure that consistency signals cannot detect, as they measure agreement among equally incorrect extractions.
We note that RE analysis relies on a single dataset (SciERC); generalization to other RE benchmarks remains to be validated.

\paragraph{Capability stratification.}
For NER, SJ effectiveness scales with structural complexity: on SciERC instances with 6+ entities, $\rho{=}0.547$, compared to $\rho{=}0.415$ for 1--2 entities.
The SJ advantage over logprob remains stable across sentence-length quartiles ($\Delta\rho{\approx}0.08$--$0.20$).
For RE, SJ $\rho$ increases monotonically with sentence length (Q1: 0.110 $\to$ Q4: 0.473; Fisher $z$-test $p{=}0.004$), indicating that longer, more relation-dense sentences provide richer structure for consistency-based estimation.
Both proxies are weakly correlated with F1 ($|r|{<}0.15$), confirming they capture input complexity rather than directly predicting output quality; however, entity count and sentence length are themselves moderately correlated ($\rho{=}0.650$), so they reflect overlapping rather than independent complexity dimensions.
For RE, entity count and relation count are strongly correlated ($\rho{=}0.769$) and thus reflect a single structural complexity dimension rather than independent axes.
On the high-complexity RE subset ($n{=}81$, high relation count), signals improve substantially: Voting reaches $\rho{=}0.630$, logprob $\rho{=}0.554$, and SJ $\rho{=}0.502$---all far above the full-set levels.
Richer relational structure provides more signal for consistency-based estimation, complementing the task-level boundary established by WNUT-17: structural signals are most effective within a ``sweet spot'' of sufficient model capability and sufficient output complexity.

\paragraph{Method boundary: WNUT-17.}
WNUT-17 establishes where the approach breaks down.
SJ achieves $\rho{=}0.062$ ($p{=}0.106$, not statistically significant), with 54\% of instances at zero F1.
Log-probability shows a strong \textit{negative} correlation: the model is confidently wrong on novel entities, a calibration failure that no post-hoc consistency signal can remedy.
This is a boundary of the method, not a limitation of the datasets.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Signal robustness across configurations (Spearman $\rho$). Top: temperature on Qwen SciERC. Middle: sample size on Qwen SciERC. Bottom: cross-model transfer (LLaMA CoNLL $N{=}16$, 3-seed mean $\pm\sigma$). $^\dagger$Mean over 3 seeds ($\sigma{=}0.025$; individual: 0.428, 0.424, 0.384).}
\label{tab:robustness}
\begin{tabular}{llcc}
\toprule
& & NER $\rho$ & RE $\rho$ \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{4}{l}{\textit{Temperature} (Qwen SciERC, $N{=}8$)} \\
\quad SJ & $T{=}0.7$ & 0.388 & 0.234 \\
\quad SJ & $T{=}1.0$ & 0.360 & 0.211 \\
\quad FK & $T{=}0.7$ & 0.321 & 0.184 \\
\quad FK & $T{=}1.0$ & 0.267 & 0.253 \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{4}{l}{\textit{Sample size} (Qwen SciERC, $T{=}1.0$)} \\
\quad SJ & $N{=}8$  & 0.360 & 0.211 \\
\quad SJ & $N{=}16$ & 0.412$^\dagger$ & 0.281 \\
\quad FK & $N{=}8$  & 0.267 & 0.253 \\
\quad FK & $N{=}16$ & 0.280 & 0.279 \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{4}{l}{\textit{Cross-model} (LLaMA CoNLL, $N{=}16$, 3 seeds)} \\
\quad SJ &  & $0.463{\pm}0.007$ & --- \\
\quad FK &  & $0.455{\pm}0.006$ & --- \\
\quad EM &  & $0.460{\pm}0.008$ & --- \\
\quad Voting &  & $0.458{\pm}0.003$ & --- \\
\quad Logprob &  & $0.310{\pm}0.005$ & --- \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{fig_temperature_robustness}
\caption{Temperature robustness on SciERC ($N{=}8$). Top: NER; bottom: RE. SJ maintains stable $\rho$ across $T{=}0.7$ and $T{=}1.0$, while FK shows mixed sensitivity. Logprob $T{=}0.7$ data unavailable.}
\label{fig:temperature_robustness}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Robustness analysis.}
Table~\ref{tab:robustness} and Figure~\ref{fig:temperature_robustness} report signal stability across temperature, sample size, and model choice.
\textit{Temperature.}
SJ NER $\rho$ shifts from 0.388 ($T{=}0.7$) to 0.360 ($T{=}1.0$), a difference of 0.028 whose bootstrap confidence interval includes zero.
FK shows mixed behavior: NER $\rho$ drops by 0.054, while RE $\rho$ increases by 0.069, likely reflecting reduced diversity at lower temperature interacting differently across tasks.
Across all comparisons, the SJ--FK relative ordering is preserved at both temperatures on NER (0.388 vs.\ 0.321 at $T{=}0.7$; 0.360 vs.\ 0.267 at $T{=}1.0$), indicating a stable signal hierarchy despite numerically small temperature effects.

\textit{Sample size.}
Increasing from $N{=}8$ to $N{=}16$ improves SJ on Qwen SciERC NER: $\rho$ rises from 0.360 to $0.412{\pm}0.025$ (three seeds: 0.428, 0.424, 0.384), a gain of $+0.052$.
The magnitude of $N$-scaling gains is setting-dependent---LLaMA SciERC NER yields $+0.016$ and Qwen CoNLL NER $+0.014$---though the direction is consistently positive.
LLaMA CoNLL exhibits the most uniform scaling: all four consistency signals gain $\Delta\rho{\approx}{+}0.030$ (range: $+0.027$ to $+0.032$) while logprob gains only $+0.003$ (Table~\ref{tab:quality_estimation}).
FK $N$-scaling is inconsistent: degradation on SciERC ($-0.007$ to $-0.019$) but improvement on CoNLL with LLaMA ($+0.027$), suggesting sensitivity to both model and task characteristics.
Voting confidence $N$-scaling is consistently positive ($+0.005$ on Qwen CoNLL, $+0.018$ on LLaMA SciERC, $+0.062$ on Qwen SciERC), while logprob is approximately $N$-invariant ($\Delta{\leq}0.021$).
SJ, EM, and voting confidence scale consistently across all tested settings; only FK shows setting-dependent variation, suggesting that structural and binary-agreement signals are the most robust to $N$.
All signals exhibit substantial miscalibration (ECE 0.27--0.77), indicating that translating consistency scores into well-calibrated confidence estimates remains an open challenge; voting achieves the lowest RE calibration error (ECE$\,{=}\,$0.272) while EM leads on NER (ECE$\,{=}\,$0.353).
For RE at $N{=}16$, SJ ($\rho{=}0.281$), FK ($\rho{=}0.279$), and logprob ($\rho{=}0.287$) all plateau at comparable levels, suggesting that compound entity-then-relation errors impose a ceiling that additional samples cannot overcome.

\paragraph{Cross-model transfer.}
LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct replicates the structural-over-surface ordering on SciERC NER (SJ $\rho{=}0.363$, FK $\rho{=}0.327$).
On CoNLL, the cross-model gap is minimal (Table~\ref{tab:quality_estimation}): SJ achieves $\rho{=}0.431$ (LLaMA) vs.\ 0.436 (Qwen), $\Delta{=}0.005$.
On conditional RE (non-zero F1 instances), SJ recovers to $\rho{=}0.405$ while FK drops to $\rho{=}0.259$, confirming that structural advantage is robust across both models and evaluation conditions.
At $N{=}16$, the structural-over-logprob advantage holds across all four tested settings: Qwen SciERC (Voting $\rho{=}0.411$ vs.\ logprob 0.259, $\Delta{=}{+}0.152$), Qwen CoNLL (EM $\rho{=}0.463$ vs.\ logprob 0.328, $\Delta{=}{+}0.135$), LLaMA SciERC (Voting $\rho{=}0.452$ vs.\ logprob 0.277, $\Delta{=}{+}0.175$), and LLaMA CoNLL 3-seed (SJ $\rho{=}0.463{\pm}0.007$ vs.\ logprob $0.310{\pm}0.005$, $\Delta{=}{+}0.153$).

\paragraph{Evaluation circularity.}
Leave-one-out SJ (LOO-SJ), which excludes the target sample when computing confidence, yields $\Delta\rho{=}{-}0.014$ relative to standard SJ, with a maximum per-instance $\Delta\rho$ of $3.1{\times}10^{-4}$.
Evaluation circularity is negligible.

\paragraph{Conditional filtering reveals signal divergence.}
Filtering to non-zero F1 instances reshuffles signal rankings (Figure~\ref{fig:signal_heatmap}, right).
EM emerges as the strongest conditional signal on both NER ($\rho{=}0.408$) and RE ($\rho{=}0.485$), despite ranking third on the full NER set ($\rho{=}0.295$) and last on full RE ($\rho{=}0.100$).
This reversal extends EM's CoNLL dominance: once catastrophic failures are removed, the remaining instances produce mostly well-formed outputs where binary agreement is highly informative.
Conversely, Voting and FK---which derive much of their full-set correlation from the zero-vs-non-zero distinction---drop substantially on conditional (Voting NER: $0.379{\to}0.346$; FK NER: $0.267{\to}0.176$).
Log-probability on conditional RE collapses to $\rho{=}0.002$, confirming that its full-set correlation ($\rho{=}0.247$) was driven entirely by coarse separation between zero and non-zero F1 instances.
At $N{=}16$, the divergence persists: SJ maintains $\rho{=}0.308$ on conditional RE while logprob drops to $\rho{=}{-}0.026$.
This EM advantage on the conditional set is not SciERC-specific: EM ranks first across all four tested configurations---SciERC NER ($\rho{=}0.408$), CoNLL Qwen $N{=}16$ ($\rho{=}0.466$), CoNLL LLaMA 3-seed ($\rho{=}0.462$), and SciERC RE ($\rho{=}0.485$)---despite full-set rankings ranging from \#1 (CoNLL Qwen) to \#5 (SciERC RE).
On the full set, EM is diluted by trivial agreement: instances where all $N$ samples produce identical (possibly incorrect) outputs receive EM${=}1$ regardless of quality, compressing the signal's dynamic range.
On the conditional set---where the model demonstrably produces varied outputs---exact agreement becomes the strongest quality signal: ``the model gives the same answer despite being able to produce different ones'' is a more precise indicator than set-level similarity.
The margin over SJ is largest on RE ($\Delta\rho{=}{+}0.167$), where compound extraction decisions amplify output variability, and smallest on CoNLL LLaMA ($\Delta\rho{=}{+}0.002$), where all signals converge near $\rho{\approx}0.46$.
This creates a natural complementarity: Voting and SJ are preferred on the full set (handling both trivial and non-trivial instances), while EM provides the most precise quality ranking within the non-trivial subset.

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{fig_reliability}
\caption{Reliability diagrams on SciERC ($N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$). Top: mean F1 vs.\ binned confidence; bottom: instance counts per bin. Left: NER; right: RE. All signals exhibit substantial miscalibration (ECE 0.27--0.77); EM achieves the lowest NER ECE (0.353) and voting the lowest RE ECE (0.272), while logprob is most miscalibrated (NER: 0.706, RE: 0.769).}
\label{fig:reliability}
\end{figure*}

\paragraph{Binary filtering vs.\ continuous ranking.}
The $\rho$--AUROC dissociation---EM leading AUROC on SciERC while Voting leads $\rho$; logprob leading AUROC on CoNLL while ranking last in $\rho$---reflects a fundamental distinction in how signals encode quality information.
Signals suited for binary filtering (EM, logprob) provide coarse separation between reliable and unreliable instances, while structural signals like SJ and Voting provide finer-grained ranking suited for prioritization and quality-aware aggregation.
Figure~\ref{fig:reliability} visualizes this complementarity across the difficulty spectrum.
Practitioners should select signal type based on the downstream application: binary filtering favors EM or logprob depending on task complexity; ranking-dependent decisions favor structural consistency.

\section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Practical recommendations.}
Our results suggest different signal choices depending on the deployment scenario.
For per-instance quality ranking, entity voting provides the strongest rank correlation ($\rho{=}0.38$, Table~\ref{tab:quality_estimation}), though exact match leads binary discrimination on SciERC (AUROC${=}0.749$).
When temperature or cross-condition robustness is required, SJ is preferable: its temperature sensitivity is small with bootstrap CIs including zero (Table~\ref{tab:robustness}), and it generalizes beyond entity-level structure to any set-valued output.
Under conditional filtering, EM leads on both NER and RE ($\rho{=}0.408$, $0.485$; \S\ref{sec:complexity_robustness}), extending binary-agreement advantages to the within-capability regime.
A naive logistic-regression ensemble of SJ and Voting does not improve over the best individual signal (AUROC${=}0.666$ vs.\ EM's 0.749), suggesting that the five signals capture largely overlapping information about instance difficulty.
For binary accept/reject decisions, EM is most effective on SciERC (AUROC${=}0.749$) and logprob on CoNLL (AUROC${=}0.761$ with LLaMA).
For best-of-$N$ selection, no signal reliably surpasses greedy on either task ($p{>}0.39$, 3-seed bootstrap; Table~\ref{tab:selection}).

\paragraph{Signals discriminate between instances, not within strata.}
When instances are stratified by greedy F1, within-stratum correlations approach zero for all signals.
Confidence signals capture \textit{between-instance} quality differences---identifying which inputs the model handles reliably---rather than providing fine-grained discrimination among instances of similar difficulty.
This is the complementary face of the correlation-selection gap (\S\ref{sec:selection_gap}): signals that predict input difficulty cannot rank outputs within a difficulty stratum.
The practical implication is that these signals are well-suited for routing and triage---flagging uncertain instances for human review---but not for fine-grained ranking within a difficulty tier.

\paragraph{Why quality estimators fail as selectors.}
The correlation-selection gap (\S\ref{sec:selection_gap}) reflects a fundamental information asymmetry.
Quality estimation ranks \textit{instances} by expected output quality, which consistency signals accomplish by measuring output distribution entropy: high inter-sample agreement indicates a peaked distribution and correlates with high F1.
Sample selection ranks \textit{candidates within a single instance}, requiring per-sample quality information that instance-level aggregation discards.
Our data quantify this directly.
On SciERC NER, the random baseline (0.608) falls 3.6~pp below greedy (0.644), confirming that per-instance sample variance exists; yet the oracle gap of 13.2~pp (0.776 vs.\ 0.644) shows that substantially better candidates exist among the $N$ samples, and the best signal (logprob) captures only +0.6~pp---a difference that is not statistically significant ($p{=}0.39$, 3-seed bootstrap).
The best quality estimator, Voting ($\rho{=}0.379$), selects to only 0.634---\textit{below} greedy---because its instance-level score cannot rank near-identical candidates.
On RE, where compound entity-then-relation decisions create more divergent outputs (oracle gap: 18.1~pp), no signal surpasses greedy---even log-probability, the sole per-sample signal, drops to $-$0.9~pp.
The $\rho$--AUROC dissociation illuminates the same asymmetry from a metric perspective.
On SciERC, EM achieves the highest AUROC (0.749 NER, 0.706 RE) yet ranks third or last in $\rho$; on CoNLL, logprob achieves the highest AUROC (0.761) yet the lowest $\rho$ (0.307).
In both cases, the AUROC leader provides coarse binary separation without fine-grained ranking.
Both metrics measure between-instance discrimination at different granularity; neither captures within-instance variation, explaining why even high AUROC does not translate to selection ability.

\paragraph{Task-difficulty-dependent signal selection.}
Across all three $N{=}16$ settings, the structural-over-logprob ordering holds consistently (\S\ref{sec:complexity_robustness}).
However, the \textit{optimal} signal shifts with task difficulty: EM dominates on easy tasks (CoNLL, greedy F1${>}$0.91), Voting and SJ dominate on hard tasks (SciERC, F1$\,{\approx}\,$0.66), and all signals converge when model capability is insufficient (WNUT-17, 54\% zero F1).
This ordering is model-agnostic---cross-model rankings between Qwen and LLaMA are identical---suggesting that the difficulty gradient, not model-specific behavior, determines which signal family is most informative.
Conditional filtering on SciERC confirms this pattern: removing zero-F1 instances shifts the effective difficulty toward the easy-task regime, and EM reclaims the lead ($\rho{=}0.408$ NER, $0.485$ RE) while Voting and SJ---the full-set leaders---drop substantially (Voting NER: $0.379{\to}0.346$; SJ RE: $0.211{\to}0.318$).

\paragraph{Capability boundary framework.}
Structural signals are most effective within the model's capability range.
Beyond it---RE with 44\% zero-F1 instances, WNUT-17 with 54\%---all signals converge toward zero or negative correlation.
Within the capability range, output complexity modulates signal effectiveness: the high-complexity RE subset ($n{=}81$) yields substantially stronger correlations (Voting $\rho{=}0.630$, SJ $\rho{=}0.502$) than the full set.
Conditional filtering further separates signal families: at $N{=}16$, SJ maintains $\rho{=}0.308$ on RE while logprob collapses to $\rho{=}{-}0.026$ (\S\ref{sec:complexity_robustness}).
The ``sweet spot'' for structural confidence signals is the intersection of sufficient model capability and sufficient output complexity---a regime where the model can produce varied but partially correct extractions rather than uniform failures.

\paragraph{Diminishing returns of $N$-scaling.}
Our $N{=}8$ and $N{=}16$ comparisons (Table~\ref{tab:robustness}) characterize the marginal value of additional samples for test-time scaling \cite{brown2024monkeys, snell2024scaling}.
For quality estimation, structural signals benefit consistently but sublinearly: SJ $\rho$ improves by $+0.052$ (Qwen SciERC, 3-seed mean) and $+0.032$ (LLaMA CoNLL, 3-seed mean) when doubling from $N{=}8$ to $N{=}16$, while log-probability is approximately $N$-invariant ($\Delta\rho{\leq}0.021$).
Structural signals leverage $\binom{N}{2}$ pairwise comparisons (28 pairs at $N{=}8$, 120 at $N{=}16$), but the $\rho$ improvement is far less than proportional, indicating diminishing information per additional comparison.
This asymmetry gives structural signals a relative advantage in the compute-constrained regime: at $N{=}8$, SJ already achieves $\rho{=}0.431$ on LLaMA CoNLL (vs.\ logprob $\rho{=}0.307$, $\Delta{=}{+}0.124$), and the gap \textit{widens} at $N{=}16$ ($\Delta{=}{+}0.153$) because structural signals continue to benefit from additional pairwise evidence while logprob does not.
For sample selection, additional samples increase the oracle upper bound---more draws raise the probability of a high-quality candidate---but signal-based selection remains flat because the selector's inability to identify the best candidate is a granularity limitation, not a sample size limitation.
The practical implication is that $N{=}8$ captures most of the achievable quality estimation benefit; further scaling widens rather than closes the correlation-selection gap absent stronger per-sample selectors.

\paragraph{Methodological implications.}
The decoupling of quality estimation ($\rho$), binary discrimination (AUROC), and sample selection (best-of-$N$ F1) means that evaluating confidence signals on a single metric risks selecting the wrong signal for the intended use case.
Threshold-based filtering favors EM or logprob (depending on task); ranking-dependent routing favors structural consistency; and effective best-of-$N$ selection likely requires per-sample signals such as trained verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers} that can evaluate individual outputs rather than distribution-level properties.
